summary: Specifies Generic Routing Encapsulation, a way to wrap packets of one network protocol inside packets of another, so arbitrary payloads can be carried across arbitrary delivery networks. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Like putting a letter in a bigger envelope with a different address so it can travel by another route.

questions: what is the gre header format
what is the gre protocol type field
subtitle: A simple, general way to wrap packets of any network protocol inside packets of another.

tldr.problem: Many separate 'X over Y' encapsulation schemes existed, one for each pairing of protocols, which does not scale (an O(n^2) problem).
tldr.mechanism: GRE puts a small header in front of the payload packet. Flags say which optional fields (checksum, key, sequence number, source route) follow, and a Protocol Type field says what the payload is. The result is then carried inside a delivery protocol.
tldr.outcome: Any payload can ride over any delivery protocol with one mechanism, though it may suit a specific pairing less well than a purpose-built scheme.

today: RFC 1701 is an Informational RFC from October 1994, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The memo itself points to RFC 1702 for GRE over IPv4 networks.

sections.title: The Problem GRE Addresses
sections.content:
Several proposals already existed for encapsulating one protocol over another, and others carried IP over IP for policy purposes. Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE) is very similar but more general. By ignoring many protocol-specific details it aims to reduce the encapsulation problem from O(n^2) to something more manageable, and to give a lightweight encapsulation for policy based routing.

The memo explicitly does not address when a packet should be encapsulated. It acknowledges, but does not address, the problems of mutual encapsulation described in RFC 1326. It admits that it may be less suitable where a specific 'X over Y' encapsulation has already been described.
sections.eli5: Instead of inventing a special envelope for every pair of mail systems, GRE offers one all-purpose envelope.

sections.title: How the Layers Nest
sections.content:
The packet that needs to be carried is the payload packet. It is first wrapped in a GRE packet, which may also include a route. That GRE packet is then encapsulated in another protocol, called the delivery protocol, and forwarded.

The finished packet has three parts in order: the delivery header, the GRE header, then the payload packet.
sections.eli5: The inner letter is the payload. The first envelope is the GRE header, and the outer envelope is the delivery header that the post office reads.

sections.title: The GRE Header
sections.content:
The header starts with two octets of flags and version. Bit 0 is the most significant bit. The flag bits are:

  • Checksum Present (bit 0) and Routing Present (bit 1). If either is set, BOTH the Checksum and Offset fields are present.
  • Key Present (bit 2) and Sequence Number Present (bit 3), which add the Key and Sequence Number fields.
  • Strict Source Route (bit 4), whose meaning is defined in other documents.
  • Recursion Control (bits 5 to 7), a three bit count of additional encapsulations that are permissible. It SHOULD default to zero.

Bits 5 through 12 are reserved for future use and MUST be transmitted as zero (the recursion control bits sit within that span). The Version (bits 13 to 15) MUST be 0.

The Protocol Type field (2 octets) holds the type of the payload, generally the Ethernet protocol type. The optional Checksum (2 octets) is the IP one's complement checksum of the GRE header and the payload. The Offset (2 octets) points into the Routing field. The Key (4 octets) is a number inserted by the encapsulator that the receiver may use to authenticate the source, and the Sequence Number (4 octets) is an unsigned 32 bit integer the receiver may use to establish order. How authenticity or ordering is determined is outside the scope of the memo.
sections.eli5: The GRE header has a row of on/off switches that say which extra labels are stuck on, such as a checksum, a secret key, or a counter to put packets back in order.

sections.title: Source Routing and Forwarding
sections.content:
The optional Routing field is a list of Source Route Entries (SREs). Each has an Address Family (2 octets), an SRE Offset (1 octet), an SRE Length (1 octet) and variable Routing Information. The list ends with a NULL SRE with address family 0x0000 and length 0. What the address family values and routing information mean is defined in other documents.

A system just forwarding the delivery packets normally treats GRE packets like any others. A system that receives a GRE packet should use some delivery-specific means to recognise it, may check the Key, Sequence Number and Checksum fields when their flags say they are valid, and should process the SREs. Once the source route is complete, the GRE header should be removed, the payload's TTL MUST be decremented (if one exists), and the payload is forwarded as a normal packet according to its Protocol Type.
sections.eli5: When the outer envelope reaches its stop, the post office checks any notes, opens it, and sends the inner letter on its way.

sections.title: Protocol Types
sections.content: Future protocol types must be taken from the DIX ethernet encoding, but for historical reasons some other values are also used. The table in the RFC MUST be used to identify those protocols. Examples include IP (0800), RFC 826 ARP (0806), Novell IPX (8137), DECnet Phase IV (6003) and Transparent Ethernet Bridging (6558). The RFC points readers to the IANA list of Ether Types for the complete list.
sections.eli5: A label on the inner letter says what language it is written in, so the receiver knows how to read it.
